headline: The tanker hit a riverboat. Now the port wants the ship.
summary: A tanker lost its steering Friday and hit the American Heritage, a river cruise boat docked in New Orleans. All 197 aboard survived. 32 went to hospital. The port sued the tanker's owners for at least $1 million in damage, and a judge gave federal officials control of the ship. Its owner is a subsidiary of a Chinese state company.
cover_answer: Yes. The ship itself is named, and the US now holds it.
table_question: If you break something by accident, do you still have to pay?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A big ship in New Orleans couldn't steer on Friday and bumped a riverboat tied up at the dock, and the riverboat tipped onto its side. Everyone had a life jacket on first, so all 197 people were pulled out of the river. The ship is longer than a football field and a half. The dock's owners want it to pay for the damage, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Life jackets on, then everyone out, is the order a six-year-old can hold.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one picture for the whole event, and here it is a boat on its side. The script gets the life jackets on before the boat tips, so the picture they keep is the rescue. Expect "could that happen to us?" A ship that couldn't steer hit a boat tied to a dock. It is rare, and that is why it was news.

8-12.script: A tanker lost its steering in New Orleans Friday and hit a docked riverboat, which rolled over. Everyone got out, but the dock took $1 million in damage. Ships leave, so the port sued and a judge is holding the tanker, like a teacher keeping the ball that broke a window until someone pays.
8-12.why: The teacher keeping the ball is the hold on the ship.
8-12.why_long: At ten the chain is the point: the steering fails, the boat rolls, the dock breaks, the port sues, a judge holds the ship. The teacher keeping the ball until someone pays is why you sue before the cause is known. Expect "what if it wasn't their fault?" The court decides that later. The hold just stops the ship leaving.

13-17.script: Can you sue a ship? The Port of New Orleans did, naming the tanker itself, and asked a court to seize and sell it to pay for the dock. The Coast Guard says the steering seems to have failed. The lawsuit says negligence. Second: if a machine fails, is anyone at fault?
13-17.why: A failed machine and a negligence claim. Let them argue which wins.
13-17.why_long: A sixteen-year-old can hold two true things: the steering seems to have failed, and the lawsuit says negligence. The script asks whether anyone is at fault when a machine fails, which the court will spend months on. Let them take the ship's side. Expect "will they really sell it?" The lawsuit asks for that. Nobody has ruled yet.

5-7.a: No. All 197 people got out. 32 went to the hospital, and none of them was badly hurt.

8-12.a: Its steering seems to have failed. Nobody knows why yet.

8-12.q: Why did the port sue so fast?
8-12.a: Ships sail away. Suing the same day got a judge to hold the tanker.

13-17.a: Yes. It names the tanker itself and asks the court to seize and sell it.

13-17.q: Does it matter that a Chinese company owns it?
13-17.a: Nothing reported ties the Chinese state owner to the crash.
